concepts_used: Definition and Mathematical Threshold of Special Majority under Article 368

solution.concept_anchor: Special majority dual threshold — total membership vs present and voting
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because students recall '2/3rd majority' as the marker of special majority and often stop there, forgetting that majority of total membership must also be simultaneously satisfied.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): it describes only the simple majority threshold under Article 100, not the special majority under Article 368.
Eliminate option (b): 2/3rd of members present and voting alone is insufficient — the majority of total membership condition must also be concurrently met.
Eliminate option (d): this describes absolute majority, not the dual-pronged special majority standard.
Retain option (c): it correctly states both prongs — majority of total membership AND 2/3rd of members present and voting — must be satisfied simultaneously.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The classic trap here is that students memorise '2/3rd majority' as the shorthand for special majority and overlook the concurrent requirement of majority of total membership. In a scenario where only 300 of 545 Lok Sabha members are present, 2/3rd of those present is 200 — yet 2/3rd of 545 (total membership) is approximately 364. A bill cleared by 200 votes out of 300 present would pass the 2/3rd-of-present test but fail the total-membership majority test. UPSC exploits this by presenting the 2/3rd threshold alone as a complete and correct description.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 368 prescribes a dual threshold for the special majority required to pass a constitutional amendment. A student who memorises only '2/3rd majority' has an incomplete understanding.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Majority of members present and voting describes simple majority under Article 100, applicable to ordinary legislation.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 2/3rd of members present and voting satisfies only one prong. If fewer members are present, this figure can be substantially less than the total-membership majority, making the bill constitutionally defective.
• Option (c) — Correct: Both conditions must be simultaneously satisfied — (i) majority of the total membership of the House, and (ii) 2/3rd majority of members present and voting.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: More than half of total membership is the definition of absolute majority, not special majority.

Value Addition:
• If 400 of 545 Lok Sabha members are present, the threshold is: majority of 545 = 273, AND 2/3rd of 400 = 267. Both must be crossed; 273 governs.
• Simple majority (Article 100) = majority of members present and voting (quorum being 1/10th).
• Special majority is required for constitutional amendments under Article 368 in each House independently.

solution.concept_anchor: Amendment bill initiation — no joint sitting, no state legislature origin

statement_analysis.statement: A Constitution Amendment Bill may be introduced in either House of Parliament and does not require the prior recommendation of the President.
statement_analysis.reason: Unlike Money Bills, Amendment Bills can be introduced in either House by any member without Presidential recommendation. This is a structural distinction from Articles 109 and 117.

statement_analysis.statement: If the Rajya Sabha rejects a Constitution Amendment Bill passed by the Lok Sabha, a joint sitting of both Houses may be convened to resolve the deadlock.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 108 providing for joint sittings applies only to ordinary bills, not to Constitution Amendment Bills. Rajya Sabha has an effective veto — if it rejects or stalls, the bill lapses or remains deadlocked with no joint-sitting remedy.

statement_analysis.statement: State Legislatures cannot introduce a Constitution Amendment Bill; they can only participate in the ratification stage for specified provisions.
statement_analysis.reason: The power to initiate constitutional amendments vests exclusively in Parliament. States may ratify certain categories of amendments (proviso to Article 368(2)) but cannot originate any amendment bill.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) (1 and 3 only) is a strong distractor because students who know Statement 2 is wrong but are uncertain about Statement 1 (confusing it with Money Bills needing Presidential recommendation) may wrongly eliminate Statement 1 and choose an option not including it.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Amendment Bills require no Presidential recommendation and can be introduced in either House — unlike Money Bills. Statement 1 is Correct.
Eliminate Statement 2: Article 108 joint sitting applies to ordinary bills only. No such provision exists for Amendment Bills. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3: State Legislatures have no power to initiate Amendment Bills — only Parliament does. Statement 3 is Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct; Statement 2 is incorrect — select option (b): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the principal trap. Students familiar with Article 108 know that joint sittings resolve deadlocks between the two Houses — and may mechanically apply this to Amendment Bills as well. However, this provision is explicitly restricted to ordinary bills. The absence of a joint-sitting mechanism for Amendment Bills is a deliberate constitutional design choice that gives Rajya Sabha absolute co-equal power in the amendment process, reinforcing the federal character of the Constitution.
solution.final_explanation:
The amendment procedure under Article 368 differs from ordinary legislation in several structurally important ways.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Any member of Parliament (not just a minister) may introduce an Amendment Bill in either House. Presidential recommendation is mandatory only for Money Bills (Article 117), not for Amendment Bills.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 108, which provides for joint sittings of Parliament to break a legislative deadlock, applies exclusively to ordinary bills. No analogous provision exists for Constitution Amendment Bills. Rajya Sabha's rejection results in the bill lapsing or remaining in deadlock — giving the Upper House an effective veto over constitutional change.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The constituent power to initiate amendments is Parliament's alone. State Legislatures are involved only at the ratification stage for amendments affecting federal provisions listed in the proviso to Article 368(2).

Value Addition:
• Rajya Sabha's absolute veto over Amendment Bills is a key federalism-protecting device — contrast with ordinary bills where Lok Sabha can override via joint sitting.
• Money Bills: introduced only in Lok Sabha, require Presidential recommendation, Rajya Sabha has only 14-day recommendatory role.
• Amendment Bills require special majority in each House independently — there is no concept of one House 'sending it' as in ordinary legislation.

concepts_used: Role of President in Constitutional Amendment: Article 368(2) vs Article 111

solution.concept_anchor: Presidential assent — mandatory post-24th CAA, contrast with Article 111

statement_analysis.statement: Under the original Constitution, the President had the explicit power to return a Constitution Amendment Bill for reconsideration, identical to the power exercised over ordinary bills.
statement_analysis.reason: The original Constitution did not explicitly mandate presidential assent for Amendment Bills, but neither did it expressly grant a return/veto power. The 24th CAA 1971 made assent mandatory. Saying the President had an 'explicit' return power identical to Article 111 in the original text is incorrect.

statement_analysis.statement: After the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, the President is obligated to give assent to every Constitution Amendment Bill duly passed by both Houses of Parliament and cannot return it for reconsideration.
statement_analysis.reason: The 24th CAA added the clause that the President 'shall' give assent — converting the position from ambiguous to mandatory. This was upheld in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

statement_analysis.statement: Article 111 of the Constitution, which governs presidential assent to bills, applies equally to ordinary bills and Constitution Amendment Bills.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 111 applies to ordinary bills. Constitution Amendment Bills are governed by Article 368(2), and after the 24th CAA, the President has no discretion — the Article 111 withholding/return power does not extend to Amendment Bills.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) (1 and 3 only) is deceptive because both statements appear to say something plausible about Presidential power, and a student who correctly identifies Statement 2 as true may still be uncertain which of Statements 1 and 3 are false.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 2 first — it is clearly correct (24th CAA mandated assent, Kesavananda upheld it). Since the question asks for NOT correct statements, Statement 2 cannot be an answer.
Evaluate Statement 1 — the original Constitution had no explicit power of return for Amendment Bills. The 24th CAA later mandated assent. Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3 — Article 111 does not cover Amendment Bills; Article 368 governs them separately. Statement 3 is Incorrect.

Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (c). Wait: option (c) here is '2 and 3 only'. Re-check options: (a)=1 only, (b)=1 and 3 only, (c)=2 and 3 only, (d)=2 only. Statements 1 and 3 are incorrect → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap here is conflating the pre-24th CAA position with the post-24th CAA position. Before 1971, there was genuine ambiguity about whether the President could withhold assent to an Amendment Bill — the Shankari Prasad context. After the 24th CAA, presidential assent is mandatory and non-discretionary. Students who know Article 111 applies to ordinary bills may incorrectly extend it to Amendment Bills, making Statement 3 sound plausible.
solution.final_explanation:
Presidential powers over bills are differentiated by the type of bill. Article 111 governs ordinary bills; Article 368 governs constitutional amendments — and these operate differently.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The original Constitution did not grant the President an explicit power to return Amendment Bills akin to Article 111. The position was ambiguous until the 24th CAA 1971, which made assent mandatory by inserting 'shall' — removing any discretion.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Post-24th CAA, the President must give assent to a duly passed Amendment Bill. This was challenged and upheld in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) as a valid exercise of constituent power.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 111 applies exclusively to ordinary legislation. It grants the President the power to withhold assent or return a bill for reconsideration — a power that does NOT extend to Amendment Bills under Article 368(2).

Value Addition:
• The Shankari Prasad (1951) case arose partly because the pre-24th CAA position on presidential assent was uncertain.
• The 24th CAA was a direct legislative response to the Golaknath (1967) judgment.
• For ordinary bills, the President has three options under Article 111: assent, withhold, or return (once only). For Amendment Bills post-24th CAA: only assent.

solution.concept_anchor: Judicial evolution — FR amendability from Shankari Prasad to Kesavananda
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) places Golaknath before Sajjan Singh, which is the most common confusion since both cases deal with the same Shankari Prasad precedent; students unsure of the exact years may reverse the two.
elimination_logic: Anchor on Shankari Prasad (1951) — it is always first in this sequence as the founding precedent on FR amendability.
Sajjan Singh (1965) reaffirmed Shankari Prasad — it must come before Golaknath (1967) which overruled both.
Golaknath (1967) overruled, 24th CAA (1971) was Parliament's legislative response — so CAA must follow Golaknath.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) is the terminal case upholding 24th CAA — always last in this sequence. Correct order: Shankari Prasad → Sajjan Singh → Golaknath → 24th CAA → Kesavananda → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Sajjan Singh–Golaknath sequencing is the classic temporal trap. Both cases engage the same question (can Parliament amend FRs?) and students who know only that Golaknath overruled the earlier position may incorrectly place Sajjan Singh after Golaknath, or conflate the two into a single pre-Kesavananda phase. The specific years — 1965 and 1967 — are tested precisely because they are close and the cases are thematically similar.
solution.final_explanation:
The evolution of the Supreme Court's position on the amendability of Fundamental Rights is a textbook constitutional law sequence that UPSC tests by scrambling the order.

Correct sequence: Shankari Prasad (1951) → Sajjan Singh (1965) → Golaknath (1967) → 24th CAA (1971) → Kesavananda Bharati (1973)

• Shankari Prasad (1951): First case; held that 'law' in Article 13 does not include constitutional amendments — Parliament can amend FRs.
• Sajjan Singh (1965): Reaffirmed Shankari Prasad; Parliament's constituent power to amend FRs upheld again.
• Golaknath (1967): Overruled both — held FRs are immune from parliamentary amendment; applied prospective overruling.
• 24th CAA (1971): Parliament's direct legislative response — inserted clause making presidential assent mandatory and affirming amendment power.
• Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Overruled Golaknath; FRs can be amended but subject to Basic Structure — current settled law.

Value Addition:
• Golaknath applied 'prospective overruling' — a technique borrowed from US law, used for the first time in India here.
• Kesavananda was decided by an 13-judge bench — the largest Constitutional Bench in Indian history.
• The 25th CAA (1971) and 29th CAA (1972) were also challenged in Kesavananda.

concepts_used: Basic Structure Doctrine as an Implied Limitation on Special Majority Power
42nd Constitutional Amendment Act 1976: Overreach and Judicial Correction

solution.concept_anchor: Minerva Mills — limited amending power is itself Basic Structure
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because both A and R are factually correct, and students may assume that because Minerva Mills struck down clauses added by the 42nd CAA and the 42nd CAA added those clauses, R causally explains A. However, R describes what the 42nd CAA did, not the reason Minerva Mills struck the clauses down.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? Minerva Mills (1980) did strike down Articles 368(4) and 368(5) inserted by the 42nd CAA. A is correct.
Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? The 42nd CAA 1976 did add clauses declaring amendments immune from judicial review and asserting unlimited constituent power. R is correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? R describes what the 42nd CAA inserted, but the reason Minerva Mills struck those clauses down was that judicial review of amendments and the limited nature of amending power are themselves components of Basic Structure — not merely because Parliament added them. R describes the act, not the constitutional rationale for striking it down. R does NOT explain A.
A is correct, R is correct, R does not explain A → option (b). Wait — recheck: option (b) states 'Both correct but R NOT correct explanation.' That matches. Select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is a reversed-causation design. A student reads A (Minerva Mills struck the clauses down) and R (42nd CAA inserted the clauses), and perceives a logical narrative — the clauses were struck down because they were inserted by the 42nd CAA. But this confuses the historical sequence with the constitutional rationale. The clauses were struck down not because they were inserted by the 42nd CAA but because they violated Basic Structure by attempting to exclude judicial review and assert unlimited constituent power. R describes a fact that preceded A, but it is not the legal reason for A.
solution.final_explanation:
Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) is a landmark case that reinforced the Basic Structure doctrine introduced in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

• Assertion (A): Correct. The Supreme Court in Minerva Mills struck down Articles 368(4) and 368(5), which were inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act 1976.
• Reason (R): Correct. The 42nd CAA did insert clause (4) declaring amendments immune from any court challenge and clause (5) asserting Parliament's unlimited constituent power.
• Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. While R accurately describes what the 42nd CAA did, the reason Minerva Mills invalidated those clauses was substantive — the Court held that (i) judicial review of constitutional amendments is itself part of Basic Structure, and (ii) the limited amending power of Parliament is a Basic Structure element. Parliament cannot enlarge its own constituent power by an amendment. R tells us what was amended, not why the amendment was unconstitutional.

Value Addition:
• Minerva Mills also curtailed Article 31C's extension to all DPSPs — only Articles 39(b) and (c) retained protection.
• The principle that limited amending power is itself Basic Structure means Parliament cannot use Article 368 to convert itself into a constituent assembly with unlimited power.
• This case is often paired with Kesavananda Bharati in UPSC questions on judicial review and Basic Structure.

solution.concept_anchor: I.R. Coelho — post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws subject to Basic Structure review
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students know that placing a law in the Ninth Schedule historically shielded it from judicial challenge, and may apply this older principle without accounting for the I.R. Coelho (2007) cut-off date of April 24, 1973.
elimination_logic: Identify the critical date: the amendment placing the law in the Ninth Schedule was made in 1985 — well after April 24, 1973 (the date of Kesavananda Bharati judgment).
Apply I.R. Coelho (2007): laws added to the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 are NOT immune from judicial review — courts can examine whether they violate Basic Structure or Fundamental Rights.
Eliminate option (b): the Ninth Schedule placement alone does not guarantee immunity post-1973. The court CAN review it.

Eliminate options (c) and (d): there is no 'automatic repeal' of the placing amendment, and the law is not immune merely because it was a state law. Option (a) correctly states that the court can review it because the Ninth Schedule placement occurred after April 24, 1973.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap operates on the historical principle that Ninth Schedule placement shields laws from FR challenge. This was true for pre-Kesavananda additions. I.R. Coelho (2007) drew a bright line at April 24, 1973 — the date of the Kesavananda judgment. Any law placed in the Ninth Schedule after that date can be judicially reviewed on the touchstone of Basic Structure and Fundamental Rights, even if placed there by a constitutionally valid special majority amendment. Students who know 'Ninth Schedule = immunity' without knowing the temporal limit will choose option (b).
solution.final_explanation:
The Ninth Schedule was created by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 under Article 31B. It was designed to insulate specific laws — primarily land reform legislation — from judicial challenge on grounds of violation of Fundamental Rights.

However, in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), a nine-judge Constitution Bench drew a critical temporal dividing line: laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment) can be judicially reviewed if they violate the Basic Structure of the Constitution or Fundamental Rights under Part III.

In the scenario: the state law was placed in the Ninth Schedule in 1985 — after the Coelho cut-off. Therefore:

• Option (a) — Correct: The Supreme Court can review the placement because it occurred post-April 24, 1973, and if it violates Basic Structure or FRs, the placement may be struck down.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Ninth Schedule immunity is not absolute for post-1973 entries. This is the partial-truth trap.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The amendment placing a law in the Ninth Schedule does not automatically become void; it is subject to review.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The law's origin as a state law does not affect the constitutional analysis.

Value Addition:
• Pre-April 24, 1973 Ninth Schedule entries retain immunity from FR challenge.
• Article 31B creates a legal fiction: laws in the Ninth Schedule shall not be deemed void even if inconsistent with Part III.
• The Ninth Schedule currently contains 284 entries, the vast majority being land reform laws.

formatted_presentation.display_text:

The law was challenged before a High Court on the grounds that it violated the right to equality under Part III of the Constitution. Before the High Court could decide, Parliament passed a Constitutional Amendment Act by special majority in 1985, inserting the state law into the Ninth Schedule. The petitioner argues that despite this, the Supreme Court can still examine the constitutionality of the law. Which of the following correctly describes the legal position?

(a) The Supreme Court can review the law because the insertion into the Ninth Schedule occurred after April 24, 1973, and its validity can be tested against Basic Structure and Fundamental Rights.
(b) The insertion into the Ninth Schedule by a constitutionally valid special majority amendment places the law beyond any judicial scrutiny, regardless of when the insertion was made.
(c) The Constitutional Amendment placing the law in the Ninth Schedule automatically becomes void because the underlying state law was challenged before the High Court prior to the amendment.
(d) A state law placed in the Ninth Schedule through a special majority amendment by Parliament enjoys immunity only if the state legislature also ratifies the placement.

solution.concept_anchor: Preamble — pre-Kesavananda vs post-Kesavananda status, Berubari Union case
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who know the 42nd CAA added words to the Preamble may assume all its elements have always been regarded as part of the Constitution, missing that the Berubari Union case (1960) specifically held the opposite.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: all four items relate to the Preamble's constitutional status or amendment history.
Option (a): Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held Preamble is part of the Constitution and can be amended — TRUE.
Option (b): 42nd CAA 1976 added 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity' to the Preamble by special majority — TRUE.
Option (c): Core elements of the Preamble (Sovereignty, Democracy, Republic) form part of Basic Structure and cannot be destroyed even by special majority — TRUE.

Option (d): Berubari Union Case (1960) held that the Preamble IS part of the Constitution — this is FALSE. Berubari held the OPPOSITE: the Preamble is NOT part of the Constitution. This was overruled by Kesavananda. Option (d) does not belong.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Berubari Union Case trap is classic entity-attribution confusion. Students know that Kesavananda established the Preamble as part of the Constitution, and may incorrectly attribute that same holding to Berubari Union — an earlier case that held precisely the contrary. UPSC regularly tests this by asking about the pre-Kesavananda versus post-Kesavananda position on the Preamble's status, exploiting the fact that most students remember the final settled law but not the historical evolution.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional status of the Preamble evolved through a series of judicial pronouncements.

• Option (a) — TRUE: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) definitively held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution and can be amended under Article 368 — part of the same settled law on amendment power.
• Option (b) — TRUE: The 42nd CAA 1976 inserted 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity' into the Preamble through special majority — a factually correct statement about constitutional history.
• Option (c) — TRUE: The Supreme Court has held that core Preamble concepts such as Sovereignty, Democratic Republic, and Justice constitute part of the Basic Structure — immune from abridgment even by special majority.
• Option (d) — FALSE and ODD ONE OUT: The Berubari Union Case (1960) held that the Preamble is NOT a part of the Constitution and cannot be used to expand legislative power. This position was subsequently overruled by Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

Value Addition:
• Berubari Union Case (1960) is examined under Article 3 (cession of territory) — Preamble status was a side discussion.
• The 44th CAA 1978 did NOT alter the Preamble — a common misconception.
• Only one amendment has ever changed the Preamble: the 42nd CAA 1976.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 169 simple majority — Article 3 new state simple majority

statement_analysis.statement: The creation of a new State by Parliament under Article 3 of the Constitution requires a special majority as prescribed under Article 368.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 3 requires only a simple majority in Parliament. Although it involves state interests and requires a bill to be referred to affected state legislatures for their views, the parliamentary vote itself is by simple majority — not special majority under Article 368.

statement_analysis.statement: Abolition of the Legislative Council of a State under Article 169 requires only a simple majority in Parliament, provided the State Legislature passes a resolution to that effect.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 169 explicitly provides that Parliament may, by law, abolish or create a State Legislative Council if the State Legislative Assembly passes a resolution by special majority requesting this — but Parliament itself acts by simple majority, not by special majority under Article 368.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students may assume that any change to the federal structure (creating a new state, abolishing a state's legislature) must follow the Article 368 special majority procedure, and mark both statements as correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Article 3 gives Parliament power to create new states, alter boundaries, etc. — this is by ordinary legislation requiring simple majority, not Article 368. Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Article 169 — Parliament acts by simple majority; the state assembly resolution must be by special majority but Parliament's own vote is simple majority. Statement 2 is Correct.
One statement correct, one incorrect — option (d) (Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap operates on students' assumption that any provision touching the federal structure must use special majority. Both creating a new state (Article 3) and abolishing a state's upper house (Article 169) deal with state-level constitutional changes — yet neither requires Parliament to use the Article 368 special majority. The Constitution deliberately places these as ordinary legislative acts to preserve parliamentary flexibility on reorganisation. Students who equate 'federal impact = special majority' will mark Statement 1 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
A recurring UPSC trap involves mistaking provisions that feel federal for provisions that require special majority under Article 368.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 3 empowers Parliament to create new states, change state boundaries, alter state names — all by ordinary legislation requiring simple majority. There is no Article 368 procedure involved. The President must refer the bill to affected state legislatures for their views, but Parliament is not bound by those views and acts by simple majority.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 169 provides that Parliament may by law create or abolish a state's Legislative Council. The State Legislative Assembly must first pass a resolution by a special majority (majority of total membership and 2/3rd of present and voting). However, Parliament's own vote on the enabling law is by simple majority — not the constitutional special majority.

Value Addition:
• Under Article 3, the state legislature's view is advisory only — Parliament may disregard it.
• Article 4 provides that laws under Articles 2 and 3 are not deemed constitutional amendments under Article 368 — they can be passed by simple majority.
• Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council was abolished in 1985 and recreated in 2007 — both via the Article 169 simple majority route in Parliament.

solution.concept_anchor: 44th CAA — 'armed rebellion' replacing 'internal disturbance' in Article 352
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students associate the 42nd CAA with Emergency-related provisions (given its 1976 context during the Emergency period) and may incorrectly attribute the tightening of Article 352 to that amendment rather than the corrective 44th CAA.
elimination_logic: Recall that the 42nd CAA 1976 expanded executive power during the Emergency period — it would not have tightened Article 352 safeguards.
The 44th CAA 1978 was enacted as a remedial measure post-Emergency to add safeguards — consistent with replacing 'internal disturbance' with the more precise 'armed rebellion'.
The 43rd CAA 1977 restored some civil liberties but the specific Article 352 textual change is attributed to the 44th CAA.
'Armed rebellion' replaced 'internal disturbance' under the 44th CAA 1978 — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges two adjacent constitutional amendments — the 42nd CAA (1976) and the 44th CAA (1978) — which are opposites in intent. The 42nd CAA was enacted during the Emergency and expanded governmental power. The 44th CAA was enacted after the Emergency as a corrective instrument and actually restricted the grounds for National Emergency proclamation by substituting 'armed rebellion' for the vague 'internal disturbance'. Students who associate Emergency-era amendments with the 42nd CAA may incorrectly attribute this change to that amendment.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 352 deals with National Emergency. The original text allowed proclamation on grounds of 'internal disturbance' — a phrase criticised as dangerously vague and susceptible to misuse.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The 42nd CAA 1976 expanded rather than restricted emergency powers during the Emergency period — it did not tighten Article 352.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The 43rd CAA 1977 was primarily concerned with restoring certain rights curtailed by the 42nd CAA and did not make the specific Article 352 textual substitution.
• Option (c) — Correct: The 44th CAA 1978 replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' in Article 352 — a deliberate tightening of the grounds for National Emergency. It also added procedural safeguards including written cabinet advice and Lok Sabha approval.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The 45th CAA does not exist as a relevant provision in this context.

Value Addition:
• 44th CAA 1978 also restored the right to life and personal liberty (Article 21) as non-suspendable even during Emergency.
• It removed the right to property from Fundamental Rights (Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31) — moved to Article 300A.
• Amending Article 352 (changing its text) is done under Article 368 special majority; approving an Emergency proclamation is a separate special majority under Article 352(6) itself.

solution.concept_anchor: Tenth Schedule — 52nd CAA, Kihoto Hollohan paragraph 7 struck down
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) pairs the Tenth Schedule with the 91st CAA, which is partially true (91st CAA amended the Tenth Schedule) but incorrectly implies the 91st CAA created it — the Tenth Schedule was created by the 52nd CAA.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The Ninth Schedule was created by the 1st CAA 1951, not the 10th CAA — temporal swap.
Eliminate option (b): The 91st CAA 2003 amended the Tenth Schedule regarding Council of Ministers size but did NOT create it — the 52nd CAA 1985 did.
Eliminate option (c): Kihoto Hollohan (1992) struck down Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule (which barred court jurisdiction), not Paragraph 5 — entity swap.
Retain option (d): The Tenth Schedule was added by the 52nd CAA 1985 to address anti-defection — correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) is a temporal-swap trap because the 91st CAA 2003 is genuinely associated with the Tenth Schedule (it capped Council of Ministers size and clarified defection rules) — a student who associates '91st CAA + Tenth Schedule' may choose it as the creating amendment, missing that the Tenth Schedule was created by the 52nd CAA 1985. Similarly, the Kihoto Hollohan trap in option (c) exploits the fact that students know a paragraph was struck down but may not recall whether it was Paragraph 5 or Paragraph 7.
solution.final_explanation:
The Tenth Schedule is the constitutional home of anti-defection provisions in India.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Ninth Schedule was created by the 1st Constitutional Amendment Act 1951. The 10th Amendment Act 1961 dealt with the merger of Dadra and Nagar Haveli — an entity-swap trap.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The 91st CAA 2003 amended the Tenth Schedule (fixing the Council of Ministers at 15% of House strength) but did not create it. The Tenth Schedule was inserted by the 52nd CAA 1985.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: In Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), the Supreme Court struck down Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule — which sought to bar judicial review of Speaker's decisions — not Paragraph 5. Paragraph 5 deals with the finality of Speaker's/Chairman's decision.
• Option (d) — Correct: The Tenth Schedule, containing the anti-defection law, was added to the Constitution by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985.

Value Addition:
• Kihoto Hollohan confirmed that Tenth Schedule (not being a federal provision) required only special majority — no state ratification.
• The 91st CAA 2003 also prohibited a member disqualified for defection from being appointed as a minister.
• Para 7 of Tenth Schedule attempted to oust judicial review — struck down as violating Basic Structure.

solution.concept_anchor: Reservation amendments — special majority only, no ratification

statement_analysis.statement: The 77th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1995, which inserted Article 16(4A) providing for reservation in promotion for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, required special majority in Parliament and ratification by at least half the State Legislatures.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 16(4A) is an amendment to a Fundamental Right in Part III. Amendments to Part III require only special majority — they do NOT fall under the ratification requirement listed in the proviso to Article 368(2). The 77th CAA required only special majority.

statement_analysis.statement: The 81st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2000, provided that unfilled vacancies reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes shall not be counted against the 50% ceiling on reservations in subsequent years.
statement_analysis.reason: The 81st CAA inserted Article 16(4B), allowing carry-forward of unfilled SC/ST vacancies without applying the 50% annual ceiling — a provision examined in M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006).

statement_analysis.statement: In M. Nagaraj (2006), the Supreme Court upheld the 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th CAAs but imposed conditions — including demonstration of backwardness, inadequate representation, and administrative efficiency — before invoking reservation in promotion.
statement_analysis.reason: M. Nagaraj upheld these amendments as constitutionally valid but held that the State must collect quantifiable data on backwardness, inadequacy of representation, and ensure overall efficiency — conditions the State must satisfy before providing reservation in promotion.

statement_analysis.statement: Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018) overruled M. Nagaraj's requirement of demonstrating 'backwardness' for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes seeking reservation in promotion, while retaining the condition of inadequate representation.
statement_analysis.reason: Jarnail Singh (2018) held that requiring SCs/STs to show backwardness was contrary to the Constitution's classification — SCs and STs are presumed to be backward by the Constitution itself. The inadequate representation and efficiency conditions from M. Nagaraj were retained.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is deceptive because Pair 1 sounds plausible — students may believe that amending a Fundamental Right provision affecting federally significant communities (SCs/STs) would require state ratification, making them count three correct pairs instead of three.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Pair 1: Amendments to Part III (Fundamental Rights) require only special majority — NO state ratification. The 77th CAA required only special majority. Pair 1 is Incorrect.
Evaluate Pair 2: Article 16(4B) — carry-forward of SC/ST vacancies without 50% ceiling — correctly describes the 81st CAA. Pair 2 is Correct.
Evaluate Pair 3: M. Nagaraj (2006) upheld those amendments with the three conditions stated. Pair 3 is Correct.
Evaluate Pair 4: Jarnail Singh (2018) removed the backwardness condition for SCs/STs while retaining other M. Nagaraj conditions. Pair 4 is Correct. Three pairs correct → option (b): Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in Pair 1 exploits the assumption that amendments affecting socially significant communities or altering service conditions must involve states. However, the proviso to Article 368(2) lists specific provisions requiring ratification — and Part III amendments are not among them. Students who equate 'important amendment = ratification' will mark Pair 1 as correct and conclude all four are correct, choosing option (d) instead of (b).
solution.final_explanation:
Reservation-related constitutional amendments primarily amend Articles 15 and 16 in Part III — and such amendments require only special majority in Parliament without any state ratification.

• Pair 1 — Incorrect: The 77th CAA amended Article 16 (Part III). The proviso to Article 368(2) does not include Part III amendments in the ratification requirement. Only special majority was needed — no state ratification.
• Pair 2 — Correct: The 81st CAA 2000 inserted Article 16(4B) providing that unfilled reserved vacancies from a year shall be treated as a separate class for the following year and shall not be counted against the 50% ceiling.
• Pair 3 — Correct: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006) upheld the 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th CAAs but imposed three conditions for invoking reservation in promotion: quantifiable data on backwardness, inadequacy of representation, and no adverse impact on administrative efficiency.
• Pair 4 — Correct: Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018) modified M. Nagaraj — SCs and STs need not demonstrate backwardness (Constitution already presumes this) but inadequate representation must still be shown.

Value Addition:
• The 85th CAA 2001 provided consequential seniority for SC/ST candidates promoted through reservation — also examined in M. Nagaraj.
• The 82nd CAA 2000 allowed relaxation in qualifying marks for SC/ST candidates in promotion.
• Jarnail Singh's modification was upheld by a larger bench in 2018 without reference to a Constitution Bench — an unusual procedural aspect.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 368 structure — clauses and their content correctly matched
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because it correctly places Article 368(3) with the 24th CAA mandatory assent provision (a well-known fact) but swaps the assignments of 368(1) and 368(2), which students less familiar with the clause-level structure of Article 368 may not detect.
elimination_logic: Anchor on List I item C (Article 368(3)): it was added by the 24th CAA 1971 to make presidential assent mandatory — matches List II item 3. This eliminates option (d) where C is matched to 4.
Anchor on List I item D (Article 368(4) and 368(5)): inserted by the 42nd CAA 1976, later struck down in Minerva Mills — matches List II item 4. This eliminates any option where D is matched to 3.
Distinguish 368(1) from 368(2): 368(1) vests amendment power in Parliament; 368(2) details the special majority procedure and proviso for ratification. A→1, B→2.
Correct matching: A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4 → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap functions by correctly matching the high-salience items (24th CAA and mandatory assent under 368(3); Minerva Mills and 368(4)/(5)) while swapping the less-remembered 368(1) and 368(2) descriptions. Students who rely on the two well-known anchors but haven't precisely read the Article's clause structure will be tricked into choosing option (c) or (b), which correctly place C and D but scramble A and B.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 368 is structured into distinct clauses, each with a specific function in the amendment procedure.

• A (Article 368(1)) → 1: Clause (1) vests the constituent power to amend any provision of the Constitution and the procedure therefor in Parliament, establishing Parliament's amendment authority.
• B (Article 368(2)) → 2: Clause (2) sets out the special majority procedure — majority of total membership AND 2/3rd of present and voting in each House — and its proviso lists categories requiring additional ratification by State Legislatures.
• C (Article 368(3)) → 3: Inserted by the 24th CAA 1971, this clause mandated that the President 'shall' give assent — removing any discretion and overriding the ambiguity that existed before Kesavananda.
• D (Articles 368(4) and 368(5)) → 4: Inserted by the 42nd CAA 1976, these clauses sought to make amendments immune from judicial review and asserted Parliament's unlimited constituent power. Both were struck down in Minerva Mills (1980).

Value Addition:
• Article 368 itself is amendable by special majority alone — no ratification needed (confirmed in Kesavananda).
• The Golaknath judgment (1967) prompted the 24th CAA's clause (3) insertion.
• After Minerva Mills, the text of Article 368 still bears clauses (4) and (5) — but they are judicially declared void.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 13 — 'law' definition, constitutional amendments excluded post-Kesavananda

statement_analysis.statement: Article 13(2) prohibits the State from making any law that abridges the rights conferred by Part III; this prohibition applies to both ordinary legislation and constitutional amendment acts.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the settled position is that 'law' in Article 13 does NOT include constitutional amendment acts. The 24th CAA and Kesavananda together resolved that constitutional amendments exercise constituent power, not ordinary legislative power, and are therefore not 'law' under Article 13.

statement_analysis.statement: In Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951), the Supreme Court held that 'law' in Article 13 does not include a constitutional amendment enacted under Article 368, thereby upholding Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights.
statement_analysis.reason: Shankari Prasad is the founding case on this question. The Court distinguished between ordinary legislative power (which produces 'law' under Article 13) and constituent power (which produces a constitutional amendment) — and held the latter is not 'law' under Article 13.

statement_analysis.statement: Even after the current settled legal position that constitutional amendments are not 'law' under Article 13, such amendments remain subject to the Basic Structure limitation evolved by the Supreme Court.
statement_analysis.reason: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) simultaneously held that constitutional amendments are not 'law' under Article 13 (so Article 13(2) doesn't bar them) AND that the Basic Structure doctrine independently limits what can be amended — a separate, judicially evolved constraint.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) (all three) is a strong distractor because Statements 2 and 3 are clearly correct, and Statement 1 may appear correct to students who apply a pre-Kesavananda understanding or confuse the Golaknath position (where the Court briefly treated amendments as 'law') with the current settled law.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The current settled law (post-Kesavananda 1973) holds that constitutional amendments are NOT 'law' under Article 13. Statement 1's claim that Article 13 applies to constitutional amendments contradicts this settled position. Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Shankari Prasad (1951) is the founding case holding that 'law' in Article 13 excludes constitutional amendments — Parliament can amend FRs. Statement 2 is Correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: Kesavananda Bharati maintains that while amendments are not Article 13 'law', Basic Structure independently limits Parliament's amendment power. Statement 3 is Correct.
Statements 2 and 3 correct, Statement 1 incorrect — select option (c): 2 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the Golaknath (1967) position — that case briefly held that constitutional amendments ARE 'law' under Article 13 and therefore cannot abridge FRs. Students who recall Golaknath's reasoning without tracking that it was overruled by Kesavananda (1973) will mark Statement 1 as correct. The scope-extension in Statement 1 ('applies to both ordinary legislation and constitutional amendment acts') is the precise error — it overstates Article 13's reach beyond its settled interpretation.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 13's definition of 'law' and its relationship to constitutional amendments is one of the most litigated questions in Indian constitutional history.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The current settled position (post-Kesavananda 1973) is that 'law' in Article 13 does not include constitutional amendments. Golaknath (1967) briefly held otherwise, but was overruled. Article 13 voids ordinary legislation that abridges FRs — it does not apply as a bar to constituent power exercised under Article 368.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Shankari Prasad (1951) established that the amendment power under Article 368 is constituent power, distinct from ordinary legislative power. The resulting amendment is not 'law' under Article 13(3), so Article 13(2) does not invalidate it.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Kesavananda synthesised the debate by holding that even though Article 13 doesn't apply to amendments, the Basic Structure doctrine — an independent, judicially evolved limitation — constrains Parliament. These are two separate tracks of constitutional protection.

Value Addition:
• The 24th CAA 1971 added a clause to Article 13 clarifying that nothing in Article 13 applies to Amendment Acts — codifying the Shankari Prasad position.
• Golaknath (1967) applied 'prospective overruling' — its holding was to operate only prospectively, not retrospectively invalidating past amendments.
• Three separate limitations on Parliament's amendment power: procedure (Article 368), Article 13 (ordinary legislation), Basic Structure (judicial doctrine).

solution.concept_anchor: Article 51A — Part IV-A, special majority only, no ratification
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because students may confuse Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A) with Directive Principles (Part IV) or Fundamental Rights (Part III) and assume different amendment requirements apply, or presume that provisions added during the Emergency era required special procedures.
elimination_logic: Identify what Article 51A contains: Fundamental Duties in Part IV-A — added by the 42nd CAA 1976.
Determine whether Part IV-A falls under the proviso to Article 368(2) requiring state ratification: it does not — ratification applies to federal-structure provisions like those in the proviso list.
Eliminate option (a): simple majority is for ordinary legislation, not constitutional amendments.
Eliminate option (c) and (d): state ratification is not required for Part IV-A amendments — retain option (b): special majority alone.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges Part IV-A (Fundamental Duties) with Part III (Fundamental Rights) or Part IV (DPSPs) in students' minds. Students who know that amending Fundamental Rights requires special majority may correctly identify the procedure — but may add 'state ratification' from a mistaken belief that FDs are constitutionally equivalent to or more important than DPSPs. The defining principle is clear: state ratification under the Article 368(2) proviso is required only for listed provisions relating to federal structure — Part IV-A is not in that list.
solution.final_explanation:
Fundamental Duties under Article 51A were inserted into the Constitution by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, which created Part IV-A.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Simple majority is the threshold for ordinary legislation. Amending the Constitution always requires at minimum the special majority under Article 368.
• Option (b) — Correct: Part IV-A does not fall within the proviso to Article 368(2) that lists provisions requiring additional ratification by State Legislatures. Amendments to Article 51A require only the special majority — majority of total membership AND 2/3rd of members present and voting in each House.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: State ratification is required only for specific federal-structure provisions listed in the proviso. Fundamental Duties are not among them.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: There is no constitutional requirement for a referendum for any amendment in India's constitutional scheme.

Value Addition:
• The 86th CAA 2002 added a tenth Fundamental Duty (education of child) — also by special majority without ratification.
• Fundamental Duties are not justiciable — courts cannot enforce them directly. However, they are used as interpretive aids.
• The Verma Committee (1999) recommended legal enforceability for some Fundamental Duties — this would itself require a special majority amendment.

solution.concept_anchor: 42nd CAA — Preamble amendment valid, 368(4)(5) struck down, Minerva Mills

statement_analysis.statement: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 amended the Preamble to add the words 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity', and this amendment to the Preamble was subsequently struck down by the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980).
statement_analysis.reason: The Preamble amendment (adding 'Socialist', 'Secular', 'Integrity') made by the 42nd CAA was NOT struck down in Minerva Mills. Minerva Mills struck down Articles 368(4) and 368(5) — the clauses claiming unlimited constituent power. The Preamble changes remain valid.

statement_analysis.statement: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act declared that no constitutional amendment shall be called in question in any court on any ground.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368(4) inserted by the 42nd CAA declared that no constitutional amendment shall be called in question in any court on any ground — a direct attempt to exclude judicial review.

statement_analysis.statement: In Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court held that the power to amend the Constitution conferred by Article 368 does not include the power to abrogate the Constitution or to destroy its Basic Structure.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the core holding of Minerva Mills — an extension of Kesavananda Bharati. The Court affirmed that the limited amending power is itself a Basic Structure feature and Parliament cannot convert its bounded constituent power into an unlimited one.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) (2 only) is a strong distractor because students who know Minerva Mills struck down some 42nd CAA provisions may assume Statement 1 (which mentions Minerva Mills and 42nd CAA) is correct, without carefully noting that Minerva Mills struck down 368(4) and (5), NOT the Preamble amendment.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 2: Article 368(4) inserted by 42nd CAA directly stated no court shall question any amendment — this is factually correct. Statement 2 is Correct (not the answer to 'NOT correct').
Evaluate Statement 3: Minerva Mills held that Basic Structure limits the amending power — this is the central holding. Statement 3 is Correct.

Evaluate Statement 1: The Preamble changes by 42nd CAA ('Socialist', 'Secular', 'Integrity') were NOT struck down in Minerva Mills. The case struck down 368(4) and 368(5), not the Preamble amendments. Statement 1 is Incorrect.
Only Statement 1 is NOT correct — select option (a): 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is a partial-truth trap. It correctly identifies the 42nd CAA's Preamble changes and correctly names Minerva Mills — but falsely connects them by claiming Minerva Mills struck down the Preamble amendment. A student who knows that Minerva Mills corrected the 42nd CAA's excesses may accept Statement 1 without carefully tracking which specific provisions Minerva Mills invalidated. The Preamble amendment is valid law; it is 368(4) and 368(5) that were struck down.
solution.final_explanation:
The 42nd CAA 1976 was the most sweeping constitutional amendment in India's history, enacted during the Emergency. It had multiple components with different legal fates.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect (NOT correct): The Preamble amendment adding 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity' was made by the 42nd CAA and has never been struck down. Minerva Mills (1980) invalidated Articles 368(4) and 368(5) — not the Preamble changes. This is the key distinction this question tests.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 368(4) as inserted by the 42nd CAA explicitly stated that no constitutional amendment shall be questioned in any court. This was an extraordinary attempt to exclude judicial review.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Minerva Mills reaffirmed and extended Kesavananda by holding that the limited nature of Parliament's amending power is itself a Basic Structure element — Parliament cannot by amendment give itself unlimited constituent power.

Value Addition:
• The 42nd CAA also extended the term of Lok Sabha and State Assemblies from 5 to 6 years — reversed by the 44th CAA 1978.
• Minerva Mills is significant for balancing FRs and DPSPs — it curtailed Article 31C's extension to all DPSPs.
• The Preamble amendment by 42nd CAA has been subject to political debate but never legal invalidation.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 31C — Minerva Mills curtailed extension to all DPSPs
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because both A and R are individually correct, and the 42nd CAA's extension of Article 31C followed by Minerva Mills' curtailment reads as a coherent narrative — students may think R explains A without checking whether the causal link is precisely stated.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? After Minerva Mills (1980), Article 31C's protection applies only to laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c), not to laws implementing all DPSPs. A is correct.
Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? The 25th CAA 1971 did insert Article 31C originally protecting laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c). R is correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? A describes the post-Minerva Mills position — the restricted scope of Article 31C. R describes the original insertion by the 25th CAA. But A's restricted scope exists because the 42nd CAA's extension to all DPSPs was struck down in Minerva Mills — not because the 25th CAA originally limited it to 39(b)(c). R gives the historical origin, not the legal reason for the current restricted scope. R does NOT explain A.
A correct + R correct + R does not explain A → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap functions here through misdirection: the Reason (R) is factually accurate about the 25th CAA — it did originally insert Article 31C in a limited form covering only Articles 39(b) and (c). But the current restricted scope (described in Assertion A) is a consequence of Minerva Mills striking down the 42nd CAA's expansion — not a consequence of the original 25th CAA limitation. R explains the history of Article 31C, not the reason for its current scope. A student who reads R and A as a coherent historical narrative will choose option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 to shield laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.

• Assertion (A): Correct. The current legal position, following Minerva Mills (1980), is that Article 31C's protection extends only to laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c) — not to laws implementing any or all Directive Principles.
• Reason (R): Correct. The 25th CAA 1971 did originally insert Article 31C in limited form — protecting laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) specifically.
• Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. The current restricted scope of Article 31C is not because the 25th CAA originally limited it to 39(b)(c) — that original limitation was subsequently expanded by the 42nd CAA 1976 to cover all DPSPs. Minerva Mills (1980) then struck down that expansion, restoring the restricted scope. The reason for the current position is Minerva Mills' invalidation of the 42nd CAA's extension — which R does not describe.

Value Addition:
• The 42nd CAA extended Article 31C to protect laws implementing any DPSP — struck down in Minerva Mills as violating Basic Structure.
• Kesavananda Bharati (1973) had partially upheld Article 31C — the part shielding from judicial review was invalidated even then.
• Article 31C creates a hierarchy: laws implementing Articles 39(b)(c) override Articles 14 and 19 — a constitutionally embedded priority for certain DPSPs.

solution.concept_anchor: Special majority calculation — total membership vs present and voting threshold
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because 267 is 2/3rd of 400 (present members) and students who know the 2/3rd rule but not the concurrent total-membership requirement will calculate correctly for one prong and miss the other.
elimination_logic: Identify the two prongs of special majority: (1) majority of total membership = majority of 545 = 273, and (2) 2/3rd of members present and voting = 2/3rd of 400 = 267.
Both conditions must be simultaneously satisfied. The bill passes only if it gets support exceeding BOTH 273 AND 267 — so the effective minimum is 273 (the higher threshold).
Option (a) says 267 is sufficient — this satisfies only the 2/3rd-of-present prong, not the total-membership majority. Eliminate (a).
Option (b) says 267 votes suffice — same error as (a). Option (c) correctly identifies 273 as the binding minimum because both conditions must be met and 273 is the higher threshold. Select (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap: 267 (2/3rd of 400 present) is a real number derived from one of the two correct prongs of special majority. A student who calculates 2/3rd of present members and stops there will arrive at 267 as the threshold — a number that is correct for one prong but incorrect for the overall determination. The binding threshold is 273 because it satisfies both prongs simultaneously: 273 > 267 (2/3rd of present), and 273 is the majority of 545. Both conditions are met only at or above 273.
solution.final_explanation:
The dual threshold under Article 368 requires a student to calculate both prongs and identify the binding minimum.

Given: Lok Sabha total membership = 545; Members present and voting = 400.

Prong 1 — Majority of total membership: More than half of 545 = 273 (minimum).
Prong 2 — 2/3rd of members present and voting: 2/3rd of 400 = 267 (minimum).

Both conditions must be met simultaneously. A vote of 267 crosses Prong 2 but falls short of Prong 2 requirement — wait, 267 < 273, so a vote of 267 fails Prong 1. The bill is validly passed only if support is at or above 273, because:
- 273 ≥ majority of 545 (Prong 1 satisfied)
- 273 > 267 (Prong 2 satisfied)

• Option (a) — Incorrect: 267 satisfies only the 2/3rd-of-present prong, not the total-membership majority prong.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Same error — only one prong calculated.
• Option (c) — Correct: The minimum to satisfy both prongs is 273 — majority of total membership is the binding constraint here.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: 364 would be 2/3rd of 545 — relevant for state ratification under some formulations, not required here.

Value Addition:
• The dual threshold means that higher absenteeism actually makes passage easier — with fewer members present, 2/3rd-of-present decreases but the total-membership majority remains fixed.
• Total membership of Rajya Sabha is 245; majority = 123; 2/3rd of full house = 164.
• The quorum for either House is 1/10th of its total membership — well below the special majority threshold.

(c) 273 votes — since the majority of total membership (273) exceeds two-thirds of members present and voting (267), and both conditions must be simultaneously satisfied
(d) 364 votes — being two-thirds of the total membership of the Lok Sabha

solution.concept_anchor: Right to Property — 44th CAA deleted Article 31, moved to Article 300A
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students know the 42nd CAA 1976 was the most sweeping amendment and may associate it with the removal of property as a Fundamental Right — the actual deletion occurred in the 44th CAA 1978.
elimination_logic: Recall that the Emergency-era 42nd CAA 1976 expanded, not contracted, fundamental rights removal — but property as a FR was not deleted then.
The 44th CAA 1978 was the post-Emergency corrective amendment that, among other things, deleted the Right to Property from Part III (removed Articles 19(1)(f) and 31).
Article 300A was added to provide a non-fundamental legal right to property — 'no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.'
Eliminate options (a), (c), (d) — select (b): 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap exploits the close association students make between major constitutional restructuring and the 42nd CAA. The Emergency period (1975-77) was associated with sweeping constitutional changes under the 42nd CAA, and students may incorrectly attribute the removal of the Right to Property to that amendment. In fact, the 44th CAA (1978) — a post-Emergency corrective enacted under the Janata government — made this change, converting property from a Fundamental Right to a constitutional right.
solution.final_explanation:
The Right to Property had a complex constitutional history before being removed from Part III.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The 42nd CAA 1976 did not delete the Right to Property from Fundamental Rights — it was associated with Emergency-era expansions of state power but not this specific change.
• Option (b) — Correct: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 deleted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 from Part III, removing the Right to Property from the status of a Fundamental Right. It was relocated as Article 300A — a constitutional right enforceable by law but not as a fundamental right (no direct Article 32 remedy).
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The 25th CAA 1971 added Article 31C — it restricted the right to property's challenge against DPSP-implementing laws, but did not delete the Fundamental Right.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The 1st CAA 1951 added Articles 31A and 31B to protect land reform laws from FR challenge — it did not delete property as a FR.

Value Addition:
• Article 300A right to property is enforceable by writ of mandamus in High Courts, not by Article 32 (Supreme Court) — a significant downgrade in protection.
• Property was originally guaranteed under Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 — the 44th CAA removed both.
• After removal, property became a 'constitutional right' — stronger than a statutory right but weaker than a fundamental right.

solution.concept_anchor: Amendment bill — no joint sitting, lapsing convention, independent passage

statement_analysis.statement: Each House of Parliament must independently pass a Constitution Amendment Bill by special majority — there is no provision for one House to transmit the bill to the other in the manner of ordinary legislation.
statement_analysis.reason: Both Houses must independently pass Amendment Bills by special majority. The concept of transmission or deeming passage (as with Money Bills where Lok Sabha passage is deemed after 14 days if Rajya Sabha doesn't act) does not apply to Amendment Bills.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 368 specifies that both Houses of Parliament must pass the Constitution Amendment Bill within the same parliamentary session.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368 imposes no time limit on passage — the two Houses need not pass the bill in the same session. One House may pass it, and the other may pass it in a subsequent session. The 'same session' requirement is not in Article 368.

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike Money Bills where the Rajya Sabha has only a recommendatory role after 14 days, Rajya Sabha has equal and absolute power over Constitution Amendment Bills — its rejection cannot be bypassed.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the fundamental distinction between Money Bills (Article 110, limited RS role), ordinary bills (joint sitting possible under Article 108), and Amendment Bills where Rajya Sabha's concurrence is absolute and non-negotiable — rejection causes deadlock.

statement_analysis.statement: Constitution Amendment Bills pending before one House automatically lapse upon the dissolution of the Lok Sabha, just as ordinary bills lapse on dissolution.
statement_analysis.reason: Unlike ordinary bills for which lapsing on dissolution is a clear constitutional rule, the position on Amendment Bills is ambiguous in the text of Article 368. By convention, they are treated as lapsing — but this is not explicitly stated in the Constitution, unlike for ordinary bills.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' tempts students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as correct and may also accept Statement 4 (Amendment Bills lapsing on dissolution) as correct, knowing that ordinary bills lapse — thus counting three correct and choosing (c).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Both Houses pass independently, no transmission concept for Amendment Bills — Correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Article 368 imposes no 'same session' requirement — this condition is fabricated. Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Rajya Sabha has equal and absolute veto on Amendment Bills — no joint sitting, no 14-day bypass. Correct.

Evaluate Statement 4: Constitutional text of Article 368 does not explicitly state that Amendment Bills lapse on dissolution — convention treats them as lapsing, but it is not the same clear rule as for ordinary bills. Incorrect. Two correct (Statements 1 and 3) → option (a): Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 exploits scope-extension — the rule that ordinary bills lapse on dissolution is extended to Amendment Bills as if it were equally explicit. In reality, Article 368 is silent on this question; it is convention, not explicit constitutional text, that treats Amendment Bills as lapsing. Students who apply the ordinary-bill lapsing rule mechanically to all bills will mark Statement 4 as correct. Similarly, Statement 2 extends a fictitious 'same session' requirement — plausible because expediting amendment passage in one session seems procedurally neat, but legally absent from Article 368.
solution.final_explanation:
The procedural mechanics of Constitution Amendment Bills under Article 368 differ from both Money Bills and ordinary bills in important ways.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Each House of Parliament must independently achieve special majority. There is no concept of one House being deemed to have passed a bill, or transmittal in the ordinary legislative sense.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 368 contains no 'same session' requirement. The two Houses may pass the bill in different sessions. The 1st CAA (1951) and several others were passed with both Houses meeting separately over different periods.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Rajya Sabha has co-equal and absolute power over Amendment Bills. Its rejection cannot be overcome by any joint sitting or timeout mechanism — a stark contrast with Money Bills (14-day rule) and ordinary bills (Article 108 joint sitting).
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The lapsing of Amendment Bills on dissolution is a matter of convention, not explicit constitutional provision. Article 368 does not address dissolution-lapsing for Amendment Bills, unlike the clear position for ordinary bills.

Value Addition:
• The absence of a joint-sitting remedy for Amendment Bills is frequently tested as a distinction from ordinary bills.
• This asymmetry gives Rajya Sabha a structural role as a federal chamber in the amendment process.
• The convention of Amendment Bills lapsing on dissolution has never been definitively tested in a constitutional case.

solution.concept_anchor: Two different special majorities — amending Article 352 vs approving Emergency proclamation

statement_analysis.statement: Amending the text of Article 352 of the Constitution — for example, to change the grounds on which a National Emergency may be proclaimed — requires the special majority procedure under Article 368, without any requirement of state legislature ratification.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 352 is an Emergency provision but does not fall under the proviso to Article 368(2) requiring state ratification. Amending it is done by special majority alone under Article 368 — as the 44th CAA 1978 demonstrated by substituting 'armed rebellion' for 'internal disturbance.'

statement_analysis.statement: The approval by Parliament of a Proclamation of National Emergency under Article 352(6) — which also requires a special majority — is an exercise of the constituent power under Article 368 and therefore governed by the same procedure as a constitutional amendment.
statement_analysis.reason: The parliamentary approval of an Emergency proclamation under Article 352(6) is an operational/executive power — it is Parliament exercising its oversight role over a Presidential proclamation. It is NOT an exercise of constituent power under Article 368. The two special majorities are different in nature: one amends the Constitution (Article 368), the other approves a proclamation (Article 352(6)).

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) (both correct) is deceptive because both statements involve special majority — the numerical threshold is the same — and students who focus on the procedural similarity (both need 2/3rd majority) rather than the constitutional source and nature of the power will mark both as correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The 44th CAA 1978 amended Article 352 by special majority without ratification — this is settled and well-documented. Statement 1 is Correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Approval of an Emergency proclamation under Article 352(6) is NOT constituent power under Article 368 — it is parliamentary approval of an executive act. The governing provision is Article 352(6), not Article 368. Two different constitutional provisions govern two different special majorities. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges two constitutionally distinct exercises of special majority. Both involve the same numerical threshold (majority of total membership + 2/3rd of present and voting), but one is constituent power (amending Article 352 under Article 368) and the other is operational power (Parliament approving a Presidential proclamation under Article 352(6) itself). UPSC exploits this by asking students to distinguish the source of power, not just the numerical requirement. Students who know 'Emergency needs special majority' without distinguishing the amendment context from the approval context will mark both statements as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Two distinct constitutional exercises can both require special majority thresholds but differ fundamentally in their legal nature and governing provision.

• Statement 1 — Correct: To alter the textual content of Article 352 — its grounds, conditions, or language — Parliament must use the amendment procedure under Article 368. Such a change requires special majority in both Houses without state ratification (Emergency provisions are not in the ratification list). The 44th CAA 1978 exemplifies this by replacing 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion.'
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: When Parliament approves a Proclamation of National Emergency under Article 352(6), it is not exercising constituent power. It is performing a parliamentary oversight function — checking the executive's decision to invoke emergency powers. The governing provision is Article 352(6) itself, not Article 368. The legal nature of the power is entirely different, even though the numerical majority required may appear similar.

Value Addition:
• Article 352(6): A proclamation must be approved by both Houses by special majority within one month (if issued when Lok Sabha is dissolved) or within 30 days otherwise.
• The distinction between 'amending a constitutional provision' and 'acting under a constitutional provision' recurs in many UPSC questions.
• Financial Emergency (Article 360) proclamation requires only simple majority for continuation — unlike National Emergency.

Fundamental Rights Amendability: Evolution through Judicial Pronouncements

solution.concept_anchor: Basic Structure elements — correct judicial attribution to cases
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because it correctly places Kesavananda Bharati with the Basic Structure doctrine but swaps the attribution of judicial review as Basic Structure (Minerva Mills) with Secularism as Basic Structure (Kesavananda), which students may not detect if they only remember that both concepts emerged from this period.
elimination_logic: Anchor List I item A (Kesavananda Bharati 1973): The foundational case establishing Basic Structure — correct match is List II item 2 (doctrine that Parliament cannot destroy Basic Structure even with special majority).

Anchor List I item C (Kihoto Hollohan 1992): Struck down Paragraph 7 of Tenth Schedule which barred judicial review — not a Basic Structure origin case for the doctrine itself. Matches List II item 3 (Para 7 of Tenth Schedule barring court jurisdiction struck down).
Anchor List I item D (Golaknath 1967): Held Parliament has no power to amend Fundamental Rights — matches List II item 4 (prospective overruling applied — Parliament cannot amend FRs).
List I item B (Minerva Mills 1980): Added 'limited amending power itself is Basic Structure' and struck down 368(4)(5) — matches List II item 1. Correct: A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4 → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Entity-swap operates across cases that are thematically proximate. Kesavananda and Minerva Mills are both Basic Structure cases — students who know both cases affirmed Basic Structure but cannot precisely attribute which holding belongs to which case will swap their List II entries. The distinction is subtle: Kesavananda originated Basic Structure, while Minerva Mills added that the limited amending power itself is a Basic Structure element (and struck down 368(4)(5)). Students may place Minerva Mills' contribution under Kesavananda's column and vice versa.
solution.final_explanation:
The evolution of Basic Structure doctrine across multiple landmark cases requires precise attribution.

• A (Kesavananda Bharati 1973) → 2: This is the founding case. A 13-judge bench held that while Parliament can amend any provision of the Constitution, it cannot use the amendment power to destroy the Basic Structure or essential features. This is the origin of the doctrine.
• B (Minerva Mills 1980) → 1: Minerva Mills extended Kesavananda by adding that the limited amending power conferred by Article 368 is itself part of the Basic Structure — Parliament cannot enlarge its own constituent power. It struck down Articles 368(4) and 368(5) inserted by the 42nd CAA.
• C (Kihoto Hollohan 1992) → 3: This case dealt with the Tenth Schedule. Paragraph 7, which sought to exclude judicial review of the Speaker's defection decisions, was struck down as violating Basic Structure by ousting court jurisdiction.
• D (Golaknath 1967) → 4: The Court held Parliament has no power to abridge Fundamental Rights through constitutional amendment. It applied prospective overruling — the decision was to have only future effect, not invalidating past amendments retroactively.

Value Addition:
• Free and Fair Elections, Federalism, Separation of Powers are also Basic Structure elements identified in Kesavananda and subsequent cases.
• S.R. Bommai (1994) confirmed that Secularism is a Basic Structure element.
• Basic Structure is nowhere written in the Constitution — it is entirely judge-made law.
