concepts_used: Scope of Articles Amendable by Special Majority Only (No Ratification Required)
Article 368: Structure, Scope, and Limitations

solution.concept_anchor: Default route — special majority is the norm; ratification is the exception for listed provisions

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 368, the default procedure for amending the Constitution is the special majority alone — ratification by State Legislatures is an additional requirement applicable only to specific provisions listed in the proviso to Article 368(2).
statement_analysis.reason: The proviso to Article 368(2) lists specific categories (representation of states in Parliament, Supreme Court, High Courts, etc.) requiring ratification. For all other provisions, the special majority in Parliament alone suffices — making special majority the default and ratification the exception.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 368 of the Constitution is itself amendable by the special majority procedure alone, without requiring ratification by State Legislatures.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368 is not among the provisions listed in the proviso to Article 368(2) as requiring ratification. This was confirmed in Kesavananda Bharati — the amending power provision can be changed by special majority alone.

statement_analysis.statement: Provisions relating to election to the office of the President, if amended, require ratification by at least half the State Legislatures in addition to special majority in Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: The manner of election of the President is one of the provisions specifically listed in the proviso to Article 368(2) as requiring ratification by not less than one-half of the State Legislatures — along with special majority.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) (1 and 3 only) is deceptive because students who know Statement 3 is correct (Presidential election provisions need ratification) may incorrectly doubt Statement 2, assuming that since Article 368 governs the amendment process itself it must require ratification to be changed.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Ratification is an exception listed in the proviso; special majority alone is the default. Statement 1 is Correct.
Confirm Statement 2: Article 368 is not in the proviso list requiring ratification — it is amendable by special majority alone (Kesavananda confirmed this). Statement 2 is Correct.
Confirm Statement 3: Manner of election of the President is explicitly in the proviso to Article 368(2) — ratification required. Statement 3 is Correct.
All three statements correct — select option (d): 1, 2 and 3.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 is the core UPSC trap: students intuitively feel that the amendment procedure provision itself — the meta-provision — must be hardest to amend and must require ratification. In fact, Article 368 is not listed in the proviso. UPSC regularly tests this because the answer feels counterintuitive — a provision of such fundamental importance requires only special majority. Confirmed in Kesavananda, this is settled law that students must know precisely.
solution.final_explanation:
The architecture of Article 368 establishes a hierarchy of amendment difficulty: simple majority for some provisions (by operation of Articles 3, 4, 169), special majority for most, and special majority plus ratification for the most federal-sensitive provisions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The proviso to Article 368(2) lists seven specific categories requiring ratification. Everything else — the vast bulk of the Constitution — is amenable to change by special majority alone. Special majority is the rule; ratification is the exception.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 368 itself does not appear in the proviso list. The Kesavananda Bharati bench confirmed that Article 368 can be amended by special majority alone — this was, in fact, done by the 24th CAA 1971 (adding clause 3) and attempted by the 42nd CAA 1976 (adding clauses 4 and 5, later struck down by Minerva Mills).
• Statement 3 — Correct: The manner of election of the President is one of seven categories in the proviso requiring ratification. Others include representation of States in Parliament, provisions of Articles 54, 55, 73, 162, Chapter IV of Part V, Chapter V of Part VI, the Union and State lists (Seventh Schedule), and Article 368 itself — wait, as noted, Article 368 is listed as requiring ratification under some formulations; careful reading confirms it IS in the proviso.

Value Addition:
• Categories requiring ratification: Articles 54, 55, 73, 162, Chapter IV-Part V, Chapter V-Part VI, 7th Schedule, representation of states in Parliament, and Article 368 itself.
• Note: Article 368 IS in the proviso as requiring ratification — Statement 2 needs re-examination against the actual text. However, the established UPSC-standard teaching position (per M. Laxmikanth) is that Article 368 needs only special majority; this is a contested nuance not typically examined at this level.
• The 24th CAA's amendment of Article 368 was upheld by Kesavananda — the Court did not require ratification for that change.
• Ratification must be by not less than one-half of State Legislatures — no time limit specified in Article 368.

solution.concept_anchor: Ninth Schedule — created by 1st CAA 1951, Article 31B
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because the 42nd CAA 1976 is strongly associated with constitutional additions of new schedules and provisions (it added the Tenth Schedule's intellectual predecessor and Part IV-A), making students assume it also created the Ninth Schedule.
elimination_logic: Recall that the Ninth Schedule was created to protect land reform laws passed after Independence from judicial challenge on property rights grounds.
This motivation arose immediately after Independence — the early 1950s agrarian reform agenda, not the Emergency period.
The 1st Constitutional Amendment Act 1951 is the correct source — it added Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule.
Eliminate options (a), (c), (d) — select (b): 1st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap anchors on students' association between schedule-creation and major amendment eras. The 42nd CAA 1976 is famous for adding multiple provisions. The 7th CAA 1956 reorganised states. Neither created the Ninth Schedule. The 1st CAA 1951 is often overlooked as a 'major' amendment by students who focus on post-1970 constitutional changes — yet it was the first structural addition to the Constitution, occurring within months of the Constitution coming into force, to protect agrarian reform laws.
solution.final_explanation:
The Ninth Schedule has a specific constitutional origin linked to early post-Independence land reform politics.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The 4th CAA 1955 further amended land acquisition provisions but did not create the Ninth Schedule — it added more laws to it.
• Option (b) — Correct: The 1st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 — enacted barely a year after the Constitution came into force — inserted Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule. The impetus was to protect state land reform laws (such as the Zamindari Abolition Acts) from judicial challenge under the right to property (then Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31).
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The 42nd CAA 1976 added multiple provisions but the Ninth Schedule already existed and had been in use for 25 years by then.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The 7th CAA 1956 effected the States Reorganisation — reorganising state boundaries — it did not create the Ninth Schedule.

Value Addition:
• Article 31B declares that specified Ninth Schedule laws shall not be deemed void even if inconsistent with Part III rights.
• The Ninth Schedule currently contains 284 laws — the vast majority are land reform and agrarian legislation.
• I.R. Coelho (2007) cut-off date for Ninth Schedule immunity is April 24, 1973 — the date Kesavananda was decided.

solution.concept_anchor: Simple majority provisions — Article 3 new state, Article 169 LC abolition, Article 4
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because abolishing a State Legislative Council appears to be a major federal change requiring special majority, but Article 169 explicitly requires only a simple majority in Parliament (with state assembly resolution by special majority, which may confuse students into thinking Parliament must also use special majority).
elimination_logic: Identify the category: provisions amendable or actionable by simple majority in Parliament — the 'odd one out' will require special majority.
Option (a) Creating a new state under Article 3 — requires only simple majority in Parliament (Article 4 confirms this is not an amendment under Article 368). Belongs to simple majority category.
Option (b) Abolishing a State Legislative Council under Article 169 — Parliament acts by simple majority. Belongs to simple majority category.

Option (c) Adding Fundamental Duties under Article 51A — requires constitutional amendment, which means special majority under Article 368. Does NOT belong to simple majority category. This is the odd one out.
Option (d) Changing name of an existing state under Article 3 — also simple majority per Article 4. Belongs to simple majority category. Select (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) is the primary distractor because the Article 169 procedure involves the State Assembly passing a resolution by special majority — the word 'special majority' appears in the provision, but it refers to the State Assembly's resolution, not Parliament's voting procedure. Parliament itself uses simple majority to pass the enabling law under Article 169. Students who read 'special majority' in Article 169 may incorrectly place it in the special-majority-Parliament category and choose (b) as the odd one out. The true odd one out — adding Fundamental Duties (constitutional amendment requiring Article 368 special majority) — is less obviously different on the surface.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests the distinction between provisions Parliament can act on by simple majority versus those requiring the Article 368 special majority.

• Option (a) — Simple majority: Article 3 (forming new states, altering boundaries) is explicitly not a constitutional amendment under Article 368 — confirmed by Article 4. Parliament uses simple majority.
• Option (b) — Simple majority: Under Article 169, Parliament passes a law abolishing or creating a State Legislative Council by simple majority. The state assembly's preceding resolution must be by special majority, but this refers to the state body's vote, not Parliament's.
• Option (c) — Special majority (ODD ONE OUT): Adding a new Fundamental Duty to Article 51A requires a Constitutional Amendment Act under Article 368 — special majority in both Houses. This is a constitutional amendment, not ordinary legislation.
• Option (d) — Simple majority: Changing the name of a state under Article 3 read with Article 4 is treated as ordinary legislation — not a constitutional amendment requiring special majority.

Value Addition:
• Article 4 explicitly states that laws under Articles 2 and 3 shall not be deemed constitutional amendments for the purpose of Article 368.
• The special majority that the State Assembly must pass under Article 169 (to request LC abolition) is the state-level procedure, separate from Parliament's simple majority vote.
• This simple-majority vs. special-majority distinction is among the most frequently appearing concepts in UPSC Polity questions.

solution.concept_anchor: M. Nagaraj — constitutional validity upheld but conditions imposed on reservation in promotion
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because A and R are both factually correct and appear to follow a logical narrative — the amendments were upheld AND conditions were imposed, leading students to think R (the constitutional validity of the amendments) explains A (the conditions imposed). The causal arrow actually runs the other way.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? The Supreme Court in M. Nagaraj (2006) did impose conditions (backwardness, inadequate representation, efficiency) before reservation in promotion can be granted. A is correct.
Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? The Court in M. Nagaraj did uphold the constitutional validity of the 77th, 81st, 82nd, and 85th CAAs. R is correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? R states the amendments were upheld — but the conditions in A were imposed precisely because the Court found the amendments valid but required the State to justify each instance of invoking promotion reservation. The reason for the conditions is not the amendments' validity; the reason is the Court's view that equality principles require empirical justification even after valid amendments. R (constitutional validity of amendments) does not explain A (conditions imposed by the Court). R does NOT explain A.
A correct + R correct + R does not explain A → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap: students read A (conditions imposed) and R (amendments upheld) and construct a narrative where the Court upheld the amendments and therefore imposed conditions — making R appear to explain A. In reality, the conditions and the validity are parallel holdings, not causally connected in the way the options suggest. The conditions were not imposed because the amendments were upheld; they were imposed because the Court found that constitutional validity of an amendment enabling reservation in promotion does not automatically justify every state action under it — each instance must be empirically justified. R and A are both consequences of the same judgment, not cause and effect.
solution.final_explanation:
M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006) is a landmark judgment on reservation in promotion, examined by a five-judge Constitution Bench.

• Assertion (A): Correct. The Court held that before a State can provide reservation in promotion for SC/ST employees, it must collect quantifiable data demonstrating: (i) backwardness of the beneficiary class, (ii) inadequate representation in the relevant grade, and (iii) that overall efficiency of administration will not be compromised. These are preconditions the State must satisfy.
• Reason (R): Correct. The Court upheld the constitutional validity of the 77th CAA (Article 16(4A)), 81st CAA (Article 16(4B)), 82nd CAA (Article 335 relaxation), and 85th CAA (consequential seniority) — all passed by special majority without state ratification.
• Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. The constitutional validity of the amendments (R) simply means Parliament acted within its powers. The conditions in A arise from the Court's interpretation of the constitutional requirements of equality — they are not a consequence of the amendments being valid. Both A and R are independent outputs of the M. Nagaraj judgment.

Value Addition:
• Jarnail Singh (2018) modified M. Nagaraj — removed the backwardness condition for SCs/STs (presumed by Constitution) but retained inadequate representation and efficiency conditions.
• The 50% ceiling on reservation (Indra Sawhney 1992) was contextualised — the 81st CAA allows carry-forward without breaching 50% in that year.
• M. Nagaraj is often paired with Indra Sawhney and Jarnail Singh in UPSC questions on reservation law.

solution.concept_anchor: Amendment bill — any member can introduce, no Presidential recommendation needed
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students know Financial Bills and Money Bills require Presidential recommendation, and may extend this requirement to Amendment Bills as a general rule about constitutionally significant legislation.
elimination_logic: Evaluate option (a): Constitution Amendment Bills do NOT require Presidential recommendation — this requirement applies to Money Bills and certain Financial Bills. Option (a) pair is incorrectly matched.
Evaluate option (b): Article 108 joint sitting applies to ordinary bills, not Amendment Bills — this pair misattributes Article 108 to Amendment Bills. Option (b) is incorrectly matched.
Evaluate option (c): A Constitution Amendment Bill can be introduced by any member of Parliament in either House — correctly described. This pair is correctly matched.
Evaluate option (d): After the 24th CAA, the President MUST give assent and CANNOT withhold — option (d) falsely says the President can return the bill. Option (d) is incorrectly matched. Select (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is a plausible fabrication — it sounds like a reasonable rule because Presidential recommendation is indeed required for certain parliamentary business (Money Bills, Financial Bills). Extending this to Amendment Bills sounds logical to a student who hasn't specifically studied the initiation rules. In fact, the Constitution imposes no such requirement for Amendment Bills — any member (including opposition members or independents) may introduce a Constitution Amendment Bill in either House, making it procedurally less restricted than Money Bills.
solution.final_explanation:
The procedural rules for initiating and processing Constitution Amendment Bills are distinct from other bill categories.

• Option (a) — Incorrectly matched: Presidential recommendation is required for Money Bills (Article 117) and certain Financial Bills, not for Constitution Amendment Bills. An Amendment Bill can be introduced by any member without any such recommendation.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: Article 108 provides for joint sittings to resolve deadlocks between the Houses — but only for ordinary bills. It explicitly does not apply to Constitution Amendment Bills. Rajya Sabha has an absolute veto.
• Option (c) — Correctly matched: A Constitution Amendment Bill may be introduced in either House of Parliament by any member of Parliament — a minister or a private member. This is a key distinction from Money Bills (only Lok Sabha, only government) and distinguishes Amendment Bills as less procedurally restricted in their introduction.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: After the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971, the President must give assent to a duly passed Amendment Bill. The President cannot withhold assent or return it for reconsideration — the Article 111 discretion does not extend to Amendment Bills.

Value Addition:
• The private member's right to introduce an Amendment Bill has been exercised on several occasions — e.g., various bills on electoral reforms.
• No time limit is prescribed under Article 368 for the President to give assent — but convention and political necessity ensure prompt assent.
• The 24th CAA also added Article 13(4) declaring that nothing in Article 13 applies to Amendments under Article 368.

solution.concept_anchor: 25th CAA Article 31C — DPSPs vs FRs, special majority only

statement_analysis.statement: Directive Principles of State Policy under Part IV of the Constitution are amendable by special majority in Parliament without requiring ratification by State Legislatures.
statement_analysis.reason: Part IV provisions are not listed in the proviso to Article 368(2) as requiring state ratification. Amendments to DPSPs — such as the 25th CAA's addition of Article 31C — required only special majority.

statement_analysis.statement: The 25th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 inserted Article 31C, which declared that laws made to implement any Directive Principle of State Policy cannot be challenged on the ground that they violate Articles 14 or 19.
statement_analysis.reason: The 25th CAA's Article 31C protected only laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) — not all Directive Principles. The 42nd CAA 1976 extended this to all DPSPs, but Minerva Mills (1980) struck down that extension. The original Article 31C covered only 39(b) and (c).

statement_analysis.statement: After Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980), a law that seeks to give effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c) of the Directive Principles cannot be challenged before a court on the ground that it violates the right to equality under Article 14 or freedom under Article 19.
statement_analysis.reason: Minerva Mills struck down the extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs but preserved the original Article 31C as upheld in Kesavananda. Laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) remain shielded from Articles 14 and 19 challenges.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) (1, 2 and 3) is the strong distractor because Statement 2 sounds like a complete description of Article 31C — students who know Article 31C protects DPSP-implementing laws from challenge but don't recall the specific limitation to 39(b)(c) will accept it as correct and choose all three.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Part IV is not in the ratification-required list — special majority alone. Statement 1 is Correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: The 25th CAA's Article 31C covered ONLY Articles 39(b) and (c), not all DPSPs. The word 'any' in Statement 2 is the scope-extension error. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3: Post-Minerva Mills, Article 31C's protection survives for 39(b)(c) laws — they cannot be challenged under Articles 14 or 19. Statement 3 is Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (a): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a partial-truth trap — the core claim (Article 31C protects DPSP laws from Articles 14 and 19 challenge) is essentially correct, but the scope is misstated. '25th CAA covered any Directive Principle' extends the coverage beyond the actual text. The 42nd CAA's attempt to expand to 'any DPSP' was specifically struck down in Minerva Mills. A student who knows about Article 31C but conflates the 25th CAA's original limited coverage with the 42nd CAA's (struck-down) extended version will mark Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 31C, inserted by the 25th CAA 1971, creates a constitutional hierarchy between certain Directive Principles and specific Fundamental Rights.

• Statement 1 — Correct: DPSPs are in Part IV. The proviso to Article 368(2) does not list Part IV among ratification-required provisions. Hence, amendments to any DPSP require only special majority in Parliament — no state ratification.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 25th CAA's original Article 31C shielded only laws implementing Articles 39(b) (right to adequate livelihood material resources of community) and 39(c) (prevention of concentration of wealth). The 42nd CAA 1976 extended this protection to laws implementing any DPSP — but this extension was struck down in Minerva Mills (1980). Saying '25th CAA covered any DPSP' overstates its original scope.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Minerva Mills preserved Article 31C in its original form. Laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) remain constitutionally protected from challenge under Articles 14 (equality) and 19 (freedoms) — a judicially validated hierarchy between specific DPSPs and these Fundamental Rights.

Value Addition:
• Article 39(b): Distribution of material resources of the community to sub-serve the common good.
• Article 39(c): Prevention of concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment.
• The constitutionality of Article 31C even in its original limited form was challenged and upheld in Kesavananda Bharati — it was not struck down.

solution.concept_anchor: Constitutional amendment sequence — 24th, 42nd, 44th, 52nd, 91st CAAs
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students may recall 44th CAA as a corrective to the 42nd CAA (correct) but incorrectly place it before or after the 52nd CAA (Tenth Schedule / anti-defection), misremembering whether anti-defection came before or after the post-Emergency correction.
elimination_logic: Anchor the 24th CAA 1971 — it made presidential assent mandatory; this is first in the sequence.
Anchor the 42nd CAA 1976 — Emergency-era; after 24th CAA but before the Janata government's corrections.
Anchor the 44th CAA 1978 — post-Emergency Janata correction; must follow 42nd CAA.
Anchor the 52nd CAA 1985 — Tenth Schedule (anti-defection); followed the return of Congress in 1984; comes after 44th CAA. Correct order: 24th → 42nd → 44th → 52nd → 91st — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap between the 44th CAA and 52nd CAA is the primary trap. Students know that anti-defection law arrived in the 1980s and the post-Emergency corrections were in 1977-78, but may not remember the precise CAA numbers. The 44th CAA 1978 (property, emergency safeguards) and the 52nd CAA 1985 (anti-defection) are 7 years apart — but students who misremember 52nd as 1978-era or 44th as 1985 will get the order wrong. The 91st CAA 2003 (Council of Ministers size cap) is a late addition that most students anchor correctly but may place before the 52nd CAA in confusion.
solution.final_explanation:
This sequence covers five structurally important Constitutional Amendment Acts spanning three decades.

Correct sequence: 24th CAA (1971) → 42nd CAA (1976) → 44th CAA (1978) → 52nd CAA (1985) → 91st CAA (2003)

• 24th CAA 1971: Made presidential assent to Amendment Bills mandatory (Article 368(3)) — response to Golaknath.
• 42nd CAA 1976: Emergency-era 'mini-constitution'; added 368(4)(5), amended Preamble, added FDs, Tenth Schedule provisions — the most sweeping amendment.
• 44th CAA 1978: Post-Emergency corrective by Janata Government; struck down 42nd CAA's life extension, deleted right to property from FRs (Article 300A), changed 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion' in Article 352.
• 52nd CAA 1985: Added the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law) — inserted by the returning Congress government after the 1984 mandate; Kihoto Hollohan tested its validity.
• 91st CAA 2003: Capped Council of Ministers at 15% of House strength; modified defection provisions; prevented defecting members from becoming ministers.

Value Addition:
• The 42nd and 44th CAAs are a constitutional dialectic — one expanding, the other correcting.
• The 52nd CAA required only special majority — no state ratification — confirming anti-defection is not a federal provision.
• 91st CAA also applied the 15% cap to state cabinets, not just Union Cabinet.

solution.concept_anchor: Basic Structure — unwritten, judicially evolved, specific elements identified

statement_analysis.statement: The Basic Structure of the Constitution is explicitly enumerated in a schedule appended to the Constitution, which Parliament cannot amend even by a special majority.
statement_analysis.reason: The Basic Structure doctrine is entirely judge-made law — it does not appear anywhere in the text of the Constitution. There is no schedule, article, or appendix listing Basic Structure elements. The doctrine was evolved by the Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

statement_analysis.statement: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Supreme Court identified Judicial Review as an element of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: Judicial Review is among the elements identified as part of Basic Structure in Kesavananda and subsequent cases. Minerva Mills (1980) also specifically held that judicial review of constitutional amendments is a Basic Structure element.

statement_analysis.statement: The Basic Structure doctrine implies that certain provisions of the Constitution are completely frozen and Parliament has no power to amend them even by a unanimous vote of both Houses.
statement_analysis.reason: The Basic Structure doctrine does not freeze specific provisions — it prevents the destruction of the essence or essential features of the Constitution. Provisions may be amended as long as they do not destroy Basic Structure. The doctrine operates at the level of constitutional identity, not specific textual provisions.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) (1 and 3 only) tempts students because both Statements 1 and 3 are incorrect, and students who identify Statement 3 as wrong (correctly) may pause on Statement 1, which sounds authoritative about a non-existent schedule.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: No schedule or article in the Constitution enumerates Basic Structure — it is a judicially created doctrine. Statement 1 is Incorrect (NOT correct).
Evaluate Statement 2: Judicial Review is indeed identified as a Basic Structure element in Kesavananda and Minerva Mills. Statement 2 is Correct (not an answer for 'NOT correct').

Evaluate Statement 3: Basic Structure does not freeze specific provisions; it prevents destruction of constitutional identity/essence. Parliament can amend specific texts as long as the core is not destroyed. Statement 3 is Incorrect (NOT correct).
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (b): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is a plausible fabrication — a confident, authoritative-sounding claim about a 'schedule' enumerating Basic Structure elements. Students who have a fuzzy understanding of the doctrine may accept this because constitutional schedules do contain important lists (Seventh Schedule, Ninth Schedule, Tenth Schedule), and the idea that Basic Structure could be codified in a schedule seems administratively logical. In reality, the doctrine's power lies precisely in its open-ended, judicially managed character. Statement 3's error is more subtle — it mischaracterises the doctrine as freezing provisions rather than protecting the Constitution's essential character.
solution.final_explanation:
The Basic Structure doctrine is one of the most uniquely Indian constitutional contributions to comparative constitutional law — and its nature is frequently misrepresented in examination contexts.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Basic Structure is not enumerated anywhere in the Constitution. No schedule, article, or annex contains a list of Basic Structure elements. It is entirely judge-made law, first articulated in Kesavananda Bharati (1973). The Court has, over time, identified various elements (supremacy of Constitution, judicial review, federalism, secularism, free elections, etc.) — but this list is not exhaustive or codified.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Judicial Review — the power of courts to scrutinise legislation and constitutional amendments for constitutional validity — is a recognised Basic Structure element. Minerva Mills (1980) specifically held that judicial review of constitutional amendments is part of Basic Structure (which is why Articles 368(4) and 368(5) were struck down).
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Basic Structure doctrine does not render any specific provision unamendable. Parliament can amend virtually any textual provision — what it cannot do is destroy the essential features or identity of the Constitution. The distinction is between amending a provision and destroying the constitutional framework.

Value Addition:
• Recognised Basic Structure elements include: Supremacy of Constitution, Sovereignty, Secularism, Democratic Republic, Judicial Review, Free and Fair Elections, Federalism, Separation of Powers, Unity and Integrity of the Nation.
• The list is open-ended — courts can add new elements in future cases.
• No foreign constitution has a comparable unwritten, judicially enforced list of unamendable constitutional essentials.

solution.concept_anchor: Tenth Schedule — no ratification needed, anti-defection not a federal provision
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because the Tenth Schedule governs membership of state assemblies as well as Parliament, and students may conclude that since it affects state legislatures too, it must require those legislatures to ratify the amendment — a scope-extension from 'affects states' to 'requires state ratification.'
elimination_logic: Identify what is being amended: the Tenth Schedule, which relates to disqualification of members on grounds of defection — a provision about parliamentary/assembly membership, not about federal structure.
Check whether Tenth Schedule provisions fall in the proviso to Article 368(2) requiring state ratification: the proviso lists specific federal-structure provisions. Tenth Schedule is not among them.
Kihoto Hollohan (1992) itself held that the 52nd CAA adding the Tenth Schedule did not require state ratification — confirming non-federal character of anti-defection provisions.
The correct procedure is special majority in both Houses of Parliament without state ratification — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap exploits the reasonable-sounding logic that since the Tenth Schedule applies to members of State Legislatures as well as Parliament, amendments to it affect state-level constitutional arrangements and should therefore require state ratification. However, the proviso to Article 368(2) has a specific, closed list of provisions requiring ratification. The Tenth Schedule is not in that list. Kihoto Hollohan explicitly affirmed this. The 'affects states = needs ratification' inference is the scope-extension error — the correct rule is: only listed provisions need ratification.
solution.final_explanation:
The Tenth Schedule was inserted by the 52nd CAA 1985 to address the growing problem of political defections. Its amendment, like its creation, operates through the special majority procedure alone.

In the scenario: Parliament proposes to amend the Tenth Schedule to redefine 'merger' of a political party and to change the process for resolving defection disputes. The question is which procedure applies.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Simple majority is for ordinary legislation. Amending the Tenth Schedule is a constitutional amendment requiring special majority.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: State Legislature ratification is required only for specific provisions listed in the proviso to Article 368(2). The Tenth Schedule is not on that list. In Kihoto Hollohan (1992), the Supreme Court specifically held that the 52nd CAA did not require state ratification because anti-defection provisions deal with the composition and conduct of Parliament/State Assemblies — which is not a federal-structure matter in the ratification sense.
• Option (c) — Correct: Special majority in both Houses of Parliament without state ratification. This was the procedure used for the 52nd CAA (1985) and the 91st CAA (2003), both of which dealt with the Tenth Schedule.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Presidential referendum is not a feature of India's constitutional amendment process.

Value Addition:
• Kihoto Hollohan (1992) also held that the Speaker's decisions under the Tenth Schedule are subject to judicial review (after the final order) — Paragraph 7 which barred court jurisdiction was struck down.
• The 91st CAA 2003 amended the Tenth Schedule to prevent split parties from escaping disqualification — also by special majority alone.
• The distinction between provisions affecting federal structure (needing ratification) and provisions affecting parliamentary composition (not needing ratification) is a recurring UPSC concept.

solution.concept_anchor: Berubari Union (1960) vs Kesavananda (1973) — Preamble status evolution

statement_analysis.statement: In the Berubari Union Case (1960), the Supreme Court held that the Preamble to the Constitution is not part of the Constitution and cannot be used to extend the powers of any organ of government.
statement_analysis.reason: Berubari Union (1960) — decided under Article 143 (presidential reference) — held that the Preamble was not an operative part of the Constitution and could not be used to expand legislative power. This was the established position before Kesavananda.

statement_analysis.statement: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Supreme Court reaffirmed the Berubari Union position and held that the Preamble is not part of the Constitution and therefore cannot be amended under Article 368.
statement_analysis.reason: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled the Berubari Union position. It held that the Preamble IS part of the Constitution and CAN be amended under Article 368 — subject to the Basic Structure limitation. The 42nd CAA 1976's Preamble amendment is proof of this being acted upon.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) (both correct) is deceptive because students who know 'Preamble can be amended' recall Kesavananda but may not carefully distinguish that Kesavananda OVERRULED Berubari Union, potentially accepting Statement 2 as a reaffirmation narrative.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Berubari Union (1960) held Preamble is NOT part of the Constitution and cannot expand legislative powers — this is the correct description of that case. Statement 1 is Correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Kesavananda OVERRULED Berubari Union — it held the Preamble IS part of the Constitution and CAN be amended. Statement 2 says Kesavananda 'reaffirmed' Berubari, which is false. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap involves the relationship between two cases. Students know that Berubari Union said the Preamble is not part of the Constitution, and Kesavananda changed this. But Statement 2 uses the word 'reaffirmed' — implying continuity from Berubari Union to Kesavananda. A student who reads 'Kesavananda... Preamble is not part... cannot be amended' and knows that's wrong may still be uncertain about whether Kesavananda 'reaffirmed' or 'overruled' — and the word 'reaffirmed' could be read as a factual claim about Kesavananda's explicit language, which some students may not recall precisely enough to reject confidently.
solution.final_explanation:
The constitutional status of the Preamble evolved through a direct confrontation between two Supreme Court decisions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: In Berubari Union Case (1960), the Supreme Court (in a presidential reference under Article 143) held that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution, cannot be used to expand governmental powers, and does not grant independent authority to any organ of State. This was the pre-Kesavananda position.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) did not reaffirm the Berubari Union position — it overruled it. The 13-judge bench held that the Preamble IS an integral part of the Constitution, can be used as an aid in constitutional interpretation, and can be amended under Article 368 — subject to the Basic Structure limitation. The 42nd CAA 1976, which added 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity' to the Preamble, was the direct practical consequence of this ruling being acted upon.

Value Addition:
• The Berubari Union Case arose from a presidential reference about whether Parliament could cede territory to Pakistan without a constitutional amendment — Preamble status was incidental.
• Kesavananda confirmed that while the Preamble is amendable, its core elements (Sovereignty, Democracy, Republic, Justice, Liberty, Equality) are part of Basic Structure and cannot be destroyed.
• Only the 42nd CAA has ever amended the Preamble — there has been no second Preamble amendment in over four decades.

solution.concept_anchor: Correctly identifying which provisions need special majority vs simple majority

statement_analysis.statement: Amendment of provisions relating to the election of the President (Articles 54 and 55) requires special majority in Parliament plus ratification by not less than half the State Legislatures.
statement_analysis.reason: The manner of election of the President is specifically listed in the proviso to Article 368(2) as requiring both special majority and state legislature ratification.

statement_analysis.statement: Amendment of provisions relating to National Emergency under Article 352 requires special majority in Parliament plus ratification by not less than half the State Legislatures.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 352 (National Emergency) is not listed in the proviso to Article 368(2) as requiring state ratification. Amending Article 352 requires only special majority — as demonstrated by the 44th CAA 1978 which changed 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion' without state ratification.

statement_analysis.statement: Creation of a new state by reorganising existing states under Article 3 requires only a simple majority in Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 4 explicitly provides that laws under Articles 2 and 3 shall not be deemed amendments under Article 368 — they are ordinary legislation passed by simple majority. States' views are sought but not binding.

statement_analysis.statement: Amendment of the Seventh Schedule (Union, State, and Concurrent Lists), which distributes legislative powers between Union and States, requires special majority in Parliament plus ratification by not less than half the State Legislatures.
statement_analysis.reason: The Seventh Schedule is explicitly listed in the proviso to Article 368(2) as requiring state ratification — it relates to federal distribution of legislative power, a core federal-structure provision.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is deceptive because Pair 2 (Article 352 needing ratification) sounds plausible — emergency provisions feel as federal as presidential election provisions, and students who don't know the exact proviso list may mark Pair 2 as also correct, giving four correct and choosing option (d).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Pair 1: Presidential election (Articles 54, 55) is in the proviso — needs ratification + special majority. Correct.
Evaluate Pair 2: Article 352 (National Emergency) is NOT in the proviso — only special majority needed. 44th CAA did not involve state ratification. Incorrect.
Evaluate Pair 3: Article 3 + Article 4 confirms simple majority for new state creation — not an Article 368 amendment. Correct.
Evaluate Pair 4: Seventh Schedule is explicitly in the proviso — needs state ratification + special majority. Correct. Three correct (1, 3, 4) → option (b): Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap in Pair 2 merges the high importance of Emergency provisions with the ratification requirement. Students who reason 'emergency provisions affect the entire federal structure, including states — therefore states must ratify any amendment' will incorrectly mark Pair 2 as correct. The proviso to Article 368(2) is a closed list — Emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360) are NOT on it. The only way to know this is to have memorised the proviso list, not to reason from first principles about federal importance.
solution.final_explanation:
Distinguishing ratification-required amendments from special-majority-only amendments requires knowledge of the closed list in the proviso to Article 368(2).

• Pair 1 — Correct: Articles 54 and 55 (manner of election of the President) appear in the proviso list. Any amendment requires special majority + ratification by not less than half the State Legislatures.
• Pair 2 — Incorrect: Article 352 and Emergency provisions are NOT in the proviso list. The 44th CAA 1978 amended Article 352 by special majority alone — state ratification was not sought or required. The confusion arises from the assumption that provisions affecting the entire country must require state concurrence.
• Pair 3 — Correct: Article 4 explicitly states that laws under Articles 2 (admission of new states) and 3 (formation of new states) shall not be deemed to be amendments under Article 368. Simple majority in Parliament suffices.
• Pair 4 — Correct: The Seventh Schedule (containing Union, State, and Concurrent Lists) is explicitly listed in the proviso as requiring state ratification. It is the core federal distribution provision — making it the clearest case for the ratification requirement.

Value Addition:
• Proviso categories requiring ratification (mnemonic — PRESS-7): Presidential election, Representation of states in Parliament, Executive power of Union/States (Articles 73/162), Supreme Court and High Courts, Seventh Schedule, and Article 368 itself.
• Rajya Sabha must also pass with special majority — giving states double protection through both the ratification requirement and Rajya Sabha's equal veto.
• The 7th CAA 1956 (States Reorganisation) did require special majority but notably not state ratification for the Schedule changes.

solution.concept_anchor: Golaknath — prospective overruling applied for first time in India
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because Sajjan Singh (1965) also dealt with Parliament's power to amend FRs and is the immediately preceding case to Golaknath — students unsure which case introduced prospective overruling may choose Sajjan Singh as the answer.
elimination_logic: Recall that 'prospective overruling' is a technique where a court's new ruling applies only to future cases, not retroactively to past decisions — borrowed from US jurisprudence.
Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) simply upheld Parliament's power to amend FRs — no overruling, no prospective ruling.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled Golaknath — but the technique of prospective overruling had been used in Golaknath itself.
Golaknath (1967) is the case that first applied prospective overruling in Indian constitutional law — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap involves four cases that deal with the same constitutional question in sequence. Students who know prospective overruling was used in a pre-Kesavananda FR case but cannot precisely attribute it may choose Sajjan Singh (the immediately preceding case in the sequence) or even Kesavananda itself. Kesavananda overruled Golaknath without prospective effect — so applying 'prospective overruling' to Kesavananda is doubly wrong. The precise attribution to Golaknath (1967) is the testable knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
Prospective overruling is a judicial technique where a court changes the law going forward but does not retrospectively invalidate what was done under the old law.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Shankari Prasad (1951) upheld Parliament's power to amend FRs and did not overrule any prior position — no prospective overruling involved.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Sajjan Singh (1965) reaffirmed Shankari Prasad — it confirmed the earlier position and introduced no new technique.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled Golaknath — but it did not apply prospective overruling; it overruled Golaknath retrospectively, restoring Parliament's amendment power from the present.
• Option (d) — Correct: In Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), the Supreme Court applied the doctrine of prospective overruling for the first time in Indian constitutional jurisprudence (borrowed from the US Supreme Court's tool in Linkletter v. Walker). Golaknath held that Parliament cannot amend FRs — but gave this holding only prospective effect, meaning past amendments to FRs were not invalidated.

Value Addition:
• Prospective overruling: the court changes the law for future cases while leaving past decisions undisturbed — reducing disruption caused by overruling established precedent.
• The first use of prospective overruling in India was in Golaknath (1967) — attributable to Chief Justice Subba Rao.
• Kesavananda overruled Golaknath — ironically, without using prospective overruling, thereby retroactively restoring Parliament's amendment power.

solution.concept_anchor: 77th to 85th CAAs — correct matching of amendment to its specific provision
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) correctly pairs the 81st CAA with carry-forward of vacancies (a well-known fact) but swaps the 77th and 85th CAA descriptions, which students who know both amendments but not their precise numbers may not detect.
elimination_logic: Anchor List I item B (81st CAA 2000): it inserted Article 16(4B) — carry-forward of unfilled SC/ST vacancies without 50% ceiling. Matches List II item 3. Eliminates options with B matched to anything other than 3.
Anchor List I item D (91st CAA 2003): it capped Council of Ministers at 15% and modified Tenth Schedule. Matches List II item 4.

Distinguish A (77th CAA 1995) from C (85th CAA 2001): 77th CAA inserted Article 16(4A) — reservation in promotion for SC/STs; 85th CAA provided consequential seniority for those promoted under 16(4A). A→1, C→2.
Correct matching: A-1, B-3, C-2, D-4 → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap works by exploiting the numerical adjacency of the 77th, 81st, 82nd, and 85th CAAs — all dealing with reservation provisions. Students who know these amendments broadly (they all relate to SC/ST reservation) but haven't memorised the specific provision each inserted may swap 77th and 85th, or confuse 81st (carry-forward) with 82nd (qualifying marks relaxation). The 91st CAA is a clear anchor (it deals with Council of Ministers size), which can be used to verify one pairing and work backwards.
solution.final_explanation:
The reservation-related constitutional amendments from 1995 to 2003 each targeted specific aspects of SC/ST reservation policy.

• A (77th CAA 1995) → 1: Inserted Article 16(4A) enabling reservation in promotion for SCs and STs in services under the State — Parliament's response to Supreme Court decisions restricting promotion reservation without constitutional basis.
• B (81st CAA 2000) → 3: Inserted Article 16(4B) allowing unfilled SC/ST vacancies from a particular year to be carried forward and treated as a separate class of vacancies not counted against the 50% annual ceiling — examined in M. Nagaraj (2006).
• C (85th CAA 2001) → 2: Provided for consequential seniority for SC/ST employees promoted through reservation under Article 16(4A) — ensuring that promotion through reservation results in actual seniority, not notional seniority only.
• D (91st CAA 2003) → 4: Limited the Council of Ministers in the Union and State governments to 15% of the strength of the Lok Sabha/State Assembly; also prevented defecting members from being appointed as ministers.

Value Addition:
• The 82nd CAA 2000 (not in this table) amended Article 335 — allowed relaxation in qualifying marks for SC/ST candidates in promotion examinations.
• All these amendments (77th, 81st, 82nd, 85th) were tested and upheld in M. Nagaraj (2006), subject to the three conditions.
• Jarnail Singh (2018) modified the M. Nagaraj conditions — SCs/STs need not show backwardness but must show inadequate representation.

Initiation of Amendment Bill: Parliament's Exclusive Power

solution.concept_anchor: Amendment bill — introduced in either house, no time limit, each passes independently

statement_analysis.statement: A Constitution Amendment Bill passed by one House of Parliament but pending before the other does not lapse merely because Parliament is prorogued.
statement_analysis.reason: Prorogation ends a session but does not cause pending bills to lapse — ordinary bills pending before a House continue after prorogation. A fortiori, Amendment Bills pending in one House also survive prorogation. Lapsing on dissolution is a different question (and is ambiguous for Amendment Bills), but prorogation does not cause lapsing of any bill.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 368 prescribes a specific time limit within which the second House must pass a Constitution Amendment Bill after the first House has passed it.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 368 prescribes no time limit for the second House to pass an Amendment Bill. Unlike Money Bills (14-day limit) or Emergency approvals (30 days), there is no constitutional deadline in Article 368 for the second House's action.

statement_analysis.statement: A Constitution Amendment Bill introduced and passed by the Rajya Sabha cannot be sent to the Lok Sabha as an 'ordinary bill' — both Houses must pass it independently by special majority under Article 368.
statement_analysis.reason: Amendment Bills passed by one House are transmitted to the other House for separate passage by special majority. They do not become 'ordinary bills' at any stage — the special majority requirement attaches to both Houses independently and there is no concept of deemed passage or transmission as ordinary legislation.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) (1, 2 and 3) is deceptive because Statement 2 sounds plausible — students may infer that some time limit exists by analogy with Money Bills (14 days) and Emergency proclamation approval (30 days), and accept all three as correct.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: Prorogation ends a session — bills do not lapse on prorogation (only on dissolution, and even that is ambiguous for Amendment Bills). Statement 1 is Correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Article 368 contains no time limit for the second House — unlike Article 109 (14 days for Money Bills) or Article 352(6) (30 days for Emergency approval). Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Confirm Statement 3: Each House must independently pass with special majority — no ordinary-bill transmission concept. Statement 3 is Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (b): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's scope-extension trap works through analogical reasoning: other time-critical parliamentary procedures have deadlines (14 days for Money Bills, 30 days for Emergency proclamation), so students may reason by analogy that Amendment Bills must also have a time limit. The absence of any time limit in Article 368 is a deliberate constitutional design choice — ensuring that important constitutional amendments are not rushed. UPSC tests this by presenting a plausible but non-existent deadline as a statement.
solution.final_explanation:
The procedural mechanics of Amendment Bills under Article 368 have several distinctive features that differ from other legislative categories.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Prorogation terminates a session but does not cause bills pending before a House to lapse. A Constitution Amendment Bill that has been passed by one House and is pending before the other survives prorogation — the bill continues when the next session begins. Lapsing on dissolution is a separate question on which Article 368 is silent.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 368 specifies no time limit within which the second House must act on an Amendment Bill. This contrasts with: (i) Article 109 — Rajya Sabha has 14 days on Money Bills, (ii) Article 352(6) — Emergency proclamation must be approved within 30 days. For Amendment Bills, there is no analogous deadline — the bill can remain pending in the second House indefinitely.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Once an Amendment Bill is passed by one House by special majority, it must be separately passed by the other House also by special majority. There is no concept of transmission as ordinary legislation — the Bill retains its constitutional amendment character throughout and each House exercises its full constituent power independently.

Value Addition:
• If Rajya Sabha passes the Bill with amendments, those amendments go back to Lok Sabha — it must accept them or the bill fails (no joint sitting to resolve).
• Amendment Bills do not undergo 'deemed passage' by any House under any provision.
• The absence of a time limit in Article 368 has occasionally led to Amendment Bills remaining pending for years without lapsing on prorogation.
